title: Solid-State Dealloying Enables Local Symmetry Breaking in Ternary Intermetallic Thin Films
authors: Mizuki Ohno, Reiley Dorrian, Veronica Show, Salva Salmani-Rezaie, Joseph Falson
abstract: Metastable quantum materials often occupy narrow composition windows with local symmetries distinct from competing equilibrium structures. These features open pathways for realizing qualitatively new electronic properties within a similar chemical subspace while at the same time complicating their deterministic synthesis. Here we illustrate a post-growth solid-state dealloying process using epitaxial ternary thin films in the La--Ag--Ge chemical space to realize a diffraction-averaged centrosymmetric superconducting structure. The process converts polar $P6_3mc$-LaAgGe into diffraction-averaged centrosymmetric AlB$_2$-type $P6/mmm$ La-Ag-Ge through net Ag loss during annealing at 800--900 $^\circ$C. Atomic-resolution electron microscopy reveals local Ag--Ge displacements of both signs relative to the planar configuration, consistent with local inversion-symmetry-breaking distortions. The converted films exhibit composition-dependent superconductivity with critical temperatures below 1 K and in-plane upper critical fields that exceed the weak-coupling Pauli-field estimate by a factor of approximately 6 in the thinnest superconducting films. These results establish epitaxial solid-state dealloying as a route to phase-selective synthesis of metastable phases, offering control over atomic-scale structural configurations and their interplay with emergent electronic properties.
summary: This work demonstrates that controlled solid-state dealloying can synthesize metastable, centrosymmetric superconducting phases in La-Ag-Ge thin films. By tuning the composition and structure, the researchers achieved superconducting films with enhanced upper critical fields, establishing dealloying as a powerful tool for phase-selective quantum material synthesis.
main_problem: The challenge of deterministically synthesizing metastable quantum materials whose local symmetries differ from their equilibrium states.
main_result: Epitaxial solid-state dealloying was successfully demonstrated to synthesize a metastable, centrosymmetric superconducting phase, allowing control over atomic-scale structure and emergent electronic properties.
method: The study employed post-growth solid-state dealloying on epitaxial thin films, combined with atomic-resolution electron microscopy and transport measurements.
model_or_system: The system is ternary intermetallic thin films ($	ext{La–Ag–Ge}$) grown epitaxially, undergoing a structural transition from a polar $	ext{P6}_3mc$ precursor to a centrosymmetric $	ext{AlB}_2$-type $	ext{P6/mmm}$ phase via controlled Ag loss.
key_observables: Superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$), in-plane upper critical field ($H_{c2}$), local Ag–Ge displacements, and transport parameters like RRR and carrier density ($n_{2	ext{D}}$).
important_parameters: Annealing temperature ($800–900^\circ	ext{C}$), film thickness ($t$), and chemical composition ($	ext{Ag/La}$ ratio).
main_assumptions: The structural assignment relies on the dealloying process stabilizing the $	ext{AlB}_2$-type phase, and the interpretation of $H_{c2}$ requires careful consideration of the Pauli limit and thickness effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structural transformation (polar to centrosymmetric), lattice parameter shifts, and the dependence of superconducting properties and transport measurements on composition and film thickness.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates the structural evolution via dealloying, characterizes the resulting phase using STEM and XRD, and then probes the resulting electronic properties through normal-state transport and superconducting magnetotransport measurements.
why_interesting: The ability to tune structural symmetry and electronic properties via a controlled, non-equilibrium processing route (dealloying) provides a powerful paradigm for designing novel quantum materials, relevant to understanding symmetry-protected topological phases.
